    print("Born weights:", [str(x) for x in p], " sum =", sum(p, Fraction(0)))

    h_fine = observed_entropy(q, v)
    print(f"\nfine entropy   H = {h_fine:.6f}   (= log 4 = {math.log(4):.6f})")

    # (a) merge two channels of positive weight  -> strict decrease
    f_merge = [0, 0, 1, 2]
    qc = coarse_grain(q, f_merge)
    h_c = observed_entropy(qc, v)
    print(f"\n(a) merging channels 1,2 (both weight 1/4 > 0):")
    print(f"    coarse entropy H' = {h_c:.6f}   strict decrease: {h_c < h_fine}")
    print(f"    predicted:  H' = {-0.5 * math.log(0.5) - 2 * 0.25 * math.log(0.25):.6f}")

    # (b) merge a positive-weight channel with a zero-weight channel -> equality
    v2 = [Fraction(1), Fraction(0), Fraction(0), Fraction(0)]
    p2 = [born_weight(qa, v2) for qa in q]
    print(f"\n(b) state v = {[str(x) for x in v2]}, Born weights {[str(x) for x in p2]}")
    h_fine2 = observed_entropy(q, v2)
    h_c2 = observed_entropy(coarse_grain(q, f_merge), v2)
    print(f"    fine H = {h_fine2:.6f},  coarse H' = {h_c2:.6f},  equality: {h_c2 == h_fine2}")
    print("    (equality boundary: no two channels of NONZERO weight were merged)")

    # (c) total merge into one channel -> entropy 0
    f_total = [0, 0, 0, 0]
    h_c3 = observed_entropy(coarse_grain(q, f_total), v)
    print(f"\n(c) merging everything into one channel: H' = {h_c3:.6f} "
          f"(<= {h_fine:.6f}: {h_c3 <= h_fine})")

    # Sharp criterion check across all merging schemes of a 4-element set.
    print("\nSharp equality criterion, checked over all 4^4 merging schemes:")
    bad = 0
    for code in range(4 ** 4):
        f = [(code >> (2 * i)) & 3 for i in range(4)]
        hc = observed_entropy(coarse_grain(q, f), v)
        pw = [born_weight(qa, v) for qa in q]
        no_merge_of_positives = all(
            not (f[a] == f[b] and a != b and pw[a] != 0 and pw[b] != 0)
            for a in range(4) for b in range(4))
        equal = abs(hc - h_fine) < 1e-12
        if equal != no_merge_of_positives:
            bad += 1
    print(f"   schemes violating the criterion: {bad}   (0 means the criterion is exact)")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 6: the functional calculus survives observation
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_functional_calculus() -> None:
    banner("7.  Polynomial functional calculus: st(p(A)) = p(st(A))")

    a = hyper_matrix([[Hyper.real(2) + EPS, Hyper.real(1)],
                      [Hyper.real(-1) * EPS, Hyper.real(3)]])
    print("A =", fmt_hyper_matrix(a), "   (finite entries)")

    # p(X) = X^3 - 2X + 5
    def p_hyper(m: HMatrix) -> HMatrix:
        m2 = h_mul(m, m)
        m3 = h_mul(m2, m)
        out = h_sub(m3, h_smul(Hyper.real(2), m))
        return h_add(out, h_smul(Hyper.real(5), h_identity(len(m))))

    def p_real(m: RMatrix) -> RMatrix:
        m2 = r_mul(m, m)
        m3 = r_mul(m2, m)
        out = [[m3[i][j] - 2 * m[i][j] for j in range(len(m))] for i in range(len(m))]
        return r_add(out, [[5 * x for x in row] for row in r_identity(len(m))])

    lhs = st_matrix(p_hyper(a))
    rhs = p_real(st_matrix(a))
    print("p(X) = X^3 - 2X + 5")
    print("st(p(A)) =", fmt_real_matrix(lhs))
    print("p(st A)  =", fmt_real_matrix(rhs))
    print("equal    :", lhs == rhs)

    # Approximate annihilators become exact: B^2 - B is infinitesimal.
    b = hyper_matrix([[ONE, EPS], [ZERO, EPS * EPS]])
    b2mb = h_sub(h_mul(b, b), b)
    print("\nB =", fmt_hyper_matrix(b))
    print("B^2 - B =", fmt_hyper_matrix(b2mb), " infinitesimal:",
          is_infinitesimal_matrix(b2mb))
    sb = st_matrix(b)
    print("st(B) =", fmt_real_matrix(sb), " and st(B)^2 - st(B) = 0 exactly:",
          r_mul(sb, sb) == sb)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def main() -> None:
    print(__doc__)
    demo_eps_channel()
    demo_sharpness_if_direction()
    demo_sharpness_only_if_direction()
    demo_three_channel_quantization()
    demo_spectral_collapse()
    demo_entropy()
    demo_functional_calculus()
    banner("All demonstrations completed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

demos.name: Exact Symbolic Tour of the Descent Theorem, its Sharpness, and its Consequences
demos.description: A complete, dependency-free walkthrough of the theory in exact arithmetic. Hyperreal scalars are represented as finite Laurent series in a formal infinite element omega with rational coefficients, so that infinitesimal, appreciable and infinite parts are separated exactly and no rounding can ever mask a violation. The script exhibits an approximate projection-valued measure that is provably not an exact one (channels overlapping by an infinitesimal, total differing from the identity by an infinitesimal) and verifies that its observation is a bona fide measurement; it reconstructs the exact model guaranteed by rigidity and prints the certified infinitesimal discrepancy; it reproduces both sharpness witnesses, the 2x2 exact hyperreal projection with an infinite entry whose observation squares to something else, and the 1x1 family whose observation is a measurement although the product of its channels is infinite; it demonstrates dimension quantization on a four-dimensional three-channel example whose hyperreal traces are non-integral but whose observed traces are the integers 2, 1, 1 summing to 4; it collapses a three-line hyperreal spectral decomposition with eigenvalues 5, 5 + epsilon and -2 onto a two-line real one; it computes observed Born weights and checks entropy monotonicity together with the sharp equality criterion against all 256 merging schemes of a four-outcome measurement; and it confirms that the real polynomial functional calculus commutes with observation.
demos.code:
"""
Standard-Part Projection-Valued Measures — numerical / symbolic demonstrations.

This script is fully self-contained (standard library only) and exercises every
main result of the theory of standard-part projection-valued measures:

  1. Exact symbolic arithmetic in a non-Archimedean field: finite Laurent series
     in a formal infinite element omega with rational coefficients.  Positive
     powers of omega are infinite, negative powers are infinitesimal, and the
     standard part of a finite element is its constant coefficient.
  2. The Descent Theorem: for hyperreal matrices with no infinite entry, the
     entrywise standard parts form a projection-valued measure (PVM) if and only
     if distinct channels are orthogonal up to infinitesimals and the total is
     infinitesimally close to the identity.
  3. Redundancy of idempotency: approximate orthogonality plus approximate
     completeness already force each channel to be approximately idempotent.
  4. Sharpness of the finiteness hypothesis, in BOTH directions, with the
     explicit 2x2 and 1x1 witnesses built from omega.
  5. Dimension quantization: observed traces are natural numbers equal to the
     ranks of the observed projections, and they sum to the dimension.
  6. Rigidity: every approximate PVM is entrywise infinitesimally close to an
     exact hyperreal PVM, namely the lift of its own observation.
  7. Spectral collapse: infinitesimally separated eigenvalues merge into a
     single observed spectral line.
  8. Observed Born measure and entropy monotonicity under coarse-graining,
     including the strict case and the sharp equality boundary.

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from dataclasses import dataclass
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Callable, Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Number = Fraction | int


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  A computable non-Archimedean field: finite Laurent series in omega
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Hyper:
    """A hyperreal number represented as a finite Laurent series in omega.

    ``coeffs`` maps an integer exponent k to the rational coefficient of
    omega**k.  Positive k contributes an infinite part, k = 0 the appreciable
    part, negative k an infinitesimal part.  Zero coefficients are dropped, so
    the representation is canonical and equality is structural.
    """

    coeffs: Tuple[Tuple[int, Fraction], ...]

    # -- construction -------------------------------------------------------

    @staticmethod
    def of(d: Dict[int, Number]) -> "Hyper":
        cleaned = {k: Fraction(v) for k, v in d.items() if Fraction(v) != 0}
        return Hyper(tuple(sorted(cleaned.items())))

    @staticmethod
    def real(c: Number) -> "Hyper":
        """The image of a real (here: rational) number in the hyperreals."""
        return Hyper.of({0: c})

    @staticmethod
    def omega(power: int = 1) -> "Hyper":
        """omega**power: infinite for power > 0, infinitesimal for power < 0."""
        return Hyper.of({power: 1})

    # -- ring structure -----------------------------------------------------

    def as_dict(self) -> Dict[int, Fraction]:
        return dict(self.coeffs)

    def __add__(self, other: "Hyper") -> "Hyper":
        out = self.as_dict()
        for k, v in other.coeffs:
            out[k] = out.get(k, Fraction(0)) + v
        return Hyper.of(out)

    def __neg__(self) -> "Hyper":
        return Hyper.of({k: -v for k, v in self.coeffs})

    def __sub__(self, other: "Hyper") -> "Hyper":
        return self + (-other)

    def __mul__(self, other: "Hyper") -> "Hyper":
        out: Dict[int, Fraction] = {}
        for k1, v1 in self.coeffs:
            for k2, v2 in other.coeffs:
                out[k1 + k2] = out.get(k1 + k2, Fraction(0)) + v1 * v2
        return Hyper.of(out)

    # -- non-Archimedean predicates ----------------------------------------

    def is_infinite(self) -> bool:
        """True iff some strictly positive power of omega occurs."""
        return any(k > 0 for k, _ in self.coeffs)

    def is_finite(self) -> bool:
        return not self.is_infinite()

    def is_infinitesimal(self) -> bool:
        """True iff every occurring power of omega is strictly negative."""
        return all(k < 0 for k, _ in self.coeffs)

    def st(self) -> Fraction:
        """Standard part: the constant coefficient (0 on infinite elements)."""
        if self.is_infinite():
            return Fraction(0)
        return dict(self.coeffs).get(0, Fraction(0))

    # -- display ------------------------------------------------------------

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        if not self.coeffs:
            return "0"
        pieces: List[str] = []
        for k, v in sorted(self.coeffs, reverse=True):
            mag = "" if abs(v) == 1 and k != 0 else str(abs(v))
            sign = "-" if v < 0 else ""
            if k == 0:
                pieces.append(f"{v}")
            elif k == 1:
                pieces.append(f"{sign}{mag}w")
            elif k == -1:
                pieces.append(f"{sign}{mag or '1'}/w")
            elif k > 0:
                pieces.append(f"{sign}{mag}w^{k}")
            else:
                pieces.append(f"{sign}{mag or '1'}/w^{-k}")
        return " + ".join(pieces).replace("+ -", "- ")


ZERO = Hyper.real(0)
ONE = Hyper.real(1)
W = Hyper.omega(1)        # an infinite element
EPS = Hyper.omega(-1)     # its reciprocal: an infinitesimal

HMatrix = List[List[Hyper]]
RMatrix = List[List[Fraction]]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  Matrix algebra over the hyperreals and over the rationals
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def hyper_matrix(rows: Sequence[Sequence[Hyper]]) -> HMatrix:
    return [list(r) for r in rows]


def h_identity(n: int) -> HMatrix:
    return [[ONE if i == j else ZERO for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]


def h_zero(n: int) -> HMatrix:
    return [[ZERO for _ in range(n)] for _ in range(n)]


def h_add(a: HMatrix, b: HMatrix) -> HMatrix:
    return [[x + y for x, y in zip(ra, rb)] for ra, rb in zip(a, b)]


def h_sub(a: HMatrix, b: HMatrix) -> HMatrix:
    return [[x - y for x, y in zip(ra, rb)] for ra, rb in zip(a, b)]


def h_mul(a: HMatrix, b: HMatrix) -> HMatrix:
    n, m, p = len(a), len(b), len(b[0])
    out = [[ZERO for _ in range(p)] for _ in range(n)]
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(p):
            acc = ZERO
            for k in range(m):
                acc = acc + a[i][k] * b[k][j]
            out[i][j] = acc
    return out


def h_smul(c: Hyper, a: HMatrix) -> HMatrix:
    return [[c * x for x in row] for row in a]


def h_sum(mats: Iterable[HMatrix], n: int) -> HMatrix:
    total = h_zero(n)
    for m in mats:
        total = h_add(total, m)
    return total


def h_trace(a: HMatrix) -> Hyper:
    acc = ZERO
    for i in range(len(a)):
        acc = acc + a[i][i]
    return acc


def has_finite_entries(a: HMatrix) -> bool:
    return all(x.is_finite() for row in a for x in row)


def is_infinitesimal_matrix(a: HMatrix) -> bool:
    return all(x.is_infinitesimal() for row in a for x in row)


def approx_eq(a: HMatrix, b: HMatrix) -> bool:
    """A ~ B: the entrywise difference is infinitesimal."""
    return is_infinitesimal_matrix(h_sub(a, b))


def st_matrix(a: HMatrix) -> RMatrix:
    """The observation map: entrywise standard part."""
    return [[x.st() for x in row] for row in a]


def lift(a: RMatrix) -> HMatrix:
    """The canonical lift of a real matrix into the hyperreals."""
    return [[Hyper.real(x) for x in row] for row in a]


def r_identity(n: int) -> RMatrix:
    return [[Fraction(1) if i == j else Fraction(0) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]


def r_mul(a: RMatrix, b: RMatrix) -> RMatrix:
    n, m, p = len(a), len(b), len(b[0])
    return [[sum((a[i][k] * b[k][j] for k in range(m)), Fraction(0)) for j in range(p)]
            for i in range(n)]


def r_add(a: RMatrix, b: RMatrix) -> RMatrix:
    return [[x + y for x, y in zip(ra, rb)] for ra, rb in zip(a, b)]


def r_zero(n: int) -> RMatrix:
    return [[Fraction(0) for _ in range(n)] for _ in range(n)]


def r_trace(a: RMatrix) -> Fraction:
    return sum((a[i][i] for i in range(len(a))), Fraction(0))


def r_rank(a: RMatrix) -> int:
    """Exact rank by Gaussian elimination over the rationals."""
    m = [row[:] for row in a]
    rows, cols = len(m), len(m[0])
    rank, pivot_row = 0, 0
    for c in range(cols):
        piv = None
        for r in range(pivot_row, rows):
            if m[r][c] != 0:
                piv = r
                break
        if piv is None:
            continue
        m[pivot_row], m[piv] = m[piv], m[pivot_row]
        inv = Fraction(1) / m[pivot_row][c]
        m[pivot_row] = [x * inv for x in m[pivot_row]]
        for r in range(rows):
            if r != pivot_row and m[r][c] != 0:
                f = m[r][c]
                m[r] = [x - f * y for x, y in zip(m[r], m[pivot_row])]
        pivot_row += 1
        rank += 1
    return rank


def r_transpose(a: RMatrix) -> RMatrix:
    return [list(col) for col in zip(*a)]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  The Descent Theorem, as an executable test
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def is_real_pvm(q: Sequence[RMatrix]) -> Tuple[bool, Dict[str, bool]]:
    """Check the three defining identities of a real projection-valued measure."""
    n = len(q[0])
    idem = all(r_mul(qa, qa) == qa for qa in q)
    orth = all(r_mul(q[a], q[b]) == r_zero(n)
               for a in range(len(q)) for b in range(len(q)) if a != b)
    total = r_zero(n)
    for qa in q:
        total = r_add(total, qa)
    complete = total == r_identity(n)
    return (idem and orth and complete,
            {"idempotent": idem, "orthogonal": orth, "complete": complete})


def descent_test(p: Sequence[HMatrix]) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """The certified descent test of the theory.

    Returns the three hypotheses (F), (O), (C), whether the observation is a
    PVM, the observed ranks, and the quantization certificate sum(rank) = n.
    """
    n = len(p[0])
    finite = all(has_finite_entries(pa) for pa in p)
    orth = all(is_infinitesimal_matrix(h_mul(p[a], p[b]))
               for a in range(len(p)) for b in range(len(p)) if a != b)
    complete = approx_eq(h_sum(p, n), h_identity(n))
    observed = [st_matrix(pa) for pa in p]
    is_pvm, parts = is_real_pvm(observed)
    ranks = [r_rank(q) for q in observed]
    return {
        "finite_entries_F": finite,
        "approx_orthogonal_O": orth,
        "approx_complete_C": complete,
        "observation_is_pvm": is_pvm,
        "observation_parts": parts,
        "observed": observed,
        "ranks": ranks,
        "rank_sum": sum(ranks),
        "dimension": n,
        # The Descent Theorem: under (F), (O) and (C) hold iff the observation is a PVM.
        "descent_theorem_confirmed": (not finite) or (is_pvm == (orth and complete)),
    }


def fmt_real_matrix(a: RMatrix) -> str:
    return "[" + "; ".join(" ".join(str(x) for x in row) for row in a) + "]"


def fmt_hyper_matrix(a: HMatrix) -> str:
    return "[" + "; ".join(" , ".join(repr(x) for x in row) for row in a) + "]"


def banner(title: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 78)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 1: the epsilon-channel — approximate but not exact
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_eps_channel() -> None:
    banner("1.  The epsilon-channel: an approximate PVM that is NOT an exact one")

    p0 = hyper_matrix([[ONE, EPS], [ZERO, ZERO]])
    p1 = hyper_matrix([[ZERO, ZERO], [ZERO, ONE]])
    p = [p0, p1]

    print("P_1 =", fmt_hyper_matrix(p0))
    print("P_2 =", fmt_hyper_matrix(p1))
    print()
    print("P_1 P_2      =", fmt_hyper_matrix(h_mul(p0, p1)),
          "  (infinitesimal, but NOT zero)")
    print("P_2 P_1      =", fmt_hyper_matrix(h_mul(p1, p0)))
    print("P_1 + P_2    =", fmt_hyper_matrix(h_add(p0, p1)),
          "  (~ I, but NOT equal to I)")

    res = descent_test(p)
    print()
    print("hypothesis (F) finite entries          :", res["finite_entries_F"])
    print("hypothesis (O) approx. orthogonality   :", res["approx_orthogonal_O"])
    print("hypothesis (C) approx. completeness    :", res["approx_complete_C"])
    print("observation is a projection-valued measure:", res["observation_is_pvm"])
    print("   -> observed channels:",
          " and ".join(fmt_real_matrix(q) for q in res["observed"]))

    # Redundancy of idempotency (Theorem: (F)+(O)+(C) => P_a P_a ~ P_a).
    print()
    for a, pa in enumerate(p, start=1):
        print(f"P_{a}^2 ~ P_{a} (idempotency was never assumed):",
              approx_eq(h_mul(pa, pa), pa))

    # Dimension quantization.
    print()
    for a, pa in enumerate(p, start=1):
        print(f"st(tr P_{a}) = {h_trace(pa).st()}  =  rank st(P_{a}) = {res['ranks'][a - 1]}")
    print(f"sum of observed ranks = {res['rank_sum']} = dim = {res['dimension']}")

    # Rigidity: the exact model is the lift of the observation.
    r = [lift(q) for q in res["observed"]]
    n = len(p0)
    exact_idem = all(h_mul(ra, ra) == ra for ra in r)
    exact_orth = h_mul(r[0], r[1]) == h_zero(n) and h_mul(r[1], r[0]) == h_zero(n)
    exact_total = h_sum(r, n) == h_identity(n)
    print()
    print("RIGIDITY.  Exact model R_a = lift(st(P_a)):")
    print("   R exactly idempotent :", exact_idem)
    print("   R exactly orthogonal :", exact_orth)
    print("   R exactly complete   :", exact_total)
    print("   P_a ~ R_a for all a  :", all(approx_eq(pa, ra) for pa, ra in zip(p, r)))
    print("   entrywise difference P_1 - R_1 =",
          fmt_hyper_matrix(h_sub(p[0], r[0])), " (infinitesimal)")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 2: sharpness — infinite entries break descent in BOTH directions
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_sharpness_if_direction() -> None:
    banner("2.  Sharpness I: an EXACT hyperreal PVM whose observation is NOT a PVM")

    # P = [[2, w], [-2/w, -1]] is an exact idempotent because w * (-2/w) = -2.
    p0 = hyper_matrix([[Hyper.real(2), W],
                       [Hyper.real(-2) * EPS, Hyper.real(-1)]])
    p1 = h_sub(h_identity(2), p0)
    p = [p0, p1]

    print("P_1 =", fmt_hyper_matrix(p0), "   (contains the infinite entry w)")
    print("P_2 = I - P_1 =", fmt_hyper_matrix(p1))
    print()
    print("P_1^2 = P_1 exactly       :", h_mul(p0, p0) == p0)
    print("P_1 P_2 = 0 exactly       :", h_mul(p0, p1) == h_zero(2))
    print("P_2 P_1 = 0 exactly       :", h_mul(p1, p0) == h_zero(2))
    print("P_1 + P_2 = I exactly     :", h_add(p0, p1) == h_identity(2))
    print("  -> this is an EXACT hyperreal projection-valued measure.")

    res = descent_test(p)
    print()
    print("hypothesis (F) finite entries :", res["finite_entries_F"], " <-- FAILS")
    print("st(P_1) =", fmt_real_matrix(res["observed"][0]))
    q = res["observed"][0]
    print("st(P_1)^2 =", fmt_real_matrix(r_mul(q, q)), " != st(P_1)")
    print("observation is a PVM :", res["observation_is_pvm"], " <-- descent FAILS")
    print()
    print("Mechanism: w * (-2/w) = -2 is an appreciable quantity manufactured from")
    print("an infinite entry and an infinitesimal one.  Entrywise observation sends")
    print("both factors to 0 and loses the contribution.")


def demo_sharpness_only_if_direction() -> None:
    banner("3.  Sharpness II: a PVM observation whose channels are NOT approx. orthogonal")

    p0 = hyper_matrix([[ONE]])
    p1 = hyper_matrix([[W]])
    p = [p0, p1]

    print("P_1 = [1],  P_2 = [w]   (1x1 matrices)")
    print("st(P_1) = [1],  st(P_2) = [0]   -> an honest PVM on R^1")
    res = descent_test(p)
    print("observation is a PVM               :", res["observation_is_pvm"])
    print("P_1 P_2 = [w] is infinitesimal     :", is_infinitesimal_matrix(h_mul(p0, p1)),
          " <-- (O) FAILS badly: w is infinite")
    print("hypothesis (F) finite entries      :", res["finite_entries_F"], " <-- FAILS")
    print()
    print("So without finiteness the 'only if' direction of the Descent Theorem is false.")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 3: a three-channel example with quantization
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_three_channel_quantization() -> None:
    banner("4.  A 4-dimensional, 3-channel approximate PVM: dimension quantization")

    n, half = 4, Fraction(1, 2)
    e2 = EPS * EPS  # 1/w^2, an infinitesimal of higher order

    # Channel 1: rank-2 projection onto span(e1, e2), perturbed infinitesimally.
    p1 = h_zero(n)
    p1[0][0] = ONE
    p1[1][1] = ONE + EPS      # an infinitesimally detuned diagonal entry
    p1[0][2] = EPS
    p1[3][1] = e2

    # Channel 2: rank-1 projection onto span(e3), perturbed.
    p2 = h_zero(n)
    p2[2][2] = ONE
    p2[2][0] = Hyper.real(3) * EPS

    # Channel 3: whatever is needed to make the total exactly I minus a tiny slack.
    p3 = h_sub(h_identity(n), h_add(p1, p2))
    p3[3][3] = p3[3][3] + e2   # extra infinitesimal detuning of the total

    p = [p1, p2, p3]
    res = descent_test(p)

    print("hypothesis (F) finite entries        :", res["finite_entries_F"])
    print("hypothesis (O) approx. orthogonality :", res["approx_orthogonal_O"])
    print("hypothesis (C) approx. completeness  :", res["approx_complete_C"])
    print("observation is a PVM                 :", res["observation_is_pvm"])
    print("Descent Theorem confirmed on this input:", res["descent_theorem_confirmed"])
    print()
    for a in range(3):
        tr_h = h_trace(p[a])
        print(f"channel {a + 1}: hyperreal trace = {tr_h!r:>14}   "
              f"st(trace) = {tr_h.st()}   rank st(P) = {res['ranks'][a]}")
    print(f"\nQUANTIZATION: {' + '.join(str(r) for r in res['ranks'])} "
          f"= {res['rank_sum']} = dim R^{res['dimension']}")
    print("The hyperreal traces live in a continuum; the observed ones are integers.")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 4: spectral collapse
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_spectral_collapse() -> None:
    banner("5.  Spectral collapse: infinitesimally separated eigenvalues merge")

    # Three rank-1 channels in R^3 with eigenvalues 5, 5 + eps, and -2.
    n = 3
    chans: List[HMatrix] = []
    for i in range(n):
        m = h_zero(n)
        m[i][i] = ONE
        chans.append(m)
    lams = [Hyper.real(5), Hyper.real(5) + EPS, Hyper.real(-2)]

    a = h_zero(n)
    for lam, ch in zip(lams, chans):
        a = h_add(a, h_smul(lam, ch))

    print("eigenvalues:", ", ".join(repr(l) for l in lams))
    print("A = sum_a lambda_a P_a =", fmt_hyper_matrix(a))
    print("st(A) =", fmt_real_matrix(st_matrix(a)))
    print()
    print("observed eigenvalues:", [str(l.st()) for l in lams])
    print("channels 1 and 2 have the SAME observed eigenvalue 5, so they fuse.")

    # Coarse-grain along f: {1,2,3} -> {A, B} merging the two 5-eigenvalue channels.
    f: Callable[[int], str] = lambda i: "A" if i in (0, 1) else "B"
    coarse: Dict[str, RMatrix] = {}
    for i in range(n):
        k = f(i)
        coarse[k] = r_add(coarse.get(k, r_zero(n)), st_matrix(chans[i]))
    mu = {"A": Fraction(5), "B": Fraction(-2)}

    rebuilt = r_zero(n)
    for k, q in coarse.items():
        rebuilt = r_add(rebuilt, [[mu[k] * x for x in row] for row in q])

    print()
    for k in sorted(coarse):
        print(f"coarse channel {k}: eigenvalue {mu[k]}, projection "
              f"{fmt_real_matrix(coarse[k])}, rank {r_rank(coarse[k])}")
    print("sum_k mu_k Q_k =", fmt_real_matrix(rebuilt))
    print("equals st(A):", rebuilt == st_matrix(a))
    print()
    print("The fine 3-channel hyperreal decomposition is observed as a 2-line real one.")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 5: Born measure and entropy under coarse-graining
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def born_weight(q: RMatrix, v: Sequence[Fraction]) -> Fraction:
    """p_a = v^T Q_a v."""
    n = len(v)
    qv = [sum((q[i][j] * v[j] for j in range(n)), Fraction(0)) for i in range(n)]
    return sum((v[i] * qv[i] for i in range(n)), Fraction(0))


def eta(t: Fraction) -> float:
    """-t log t, with eta(0) = 0."""
    x = float(t)
    return 0.0 if x <= 0.0 else -x * math.log(x)


def observed_entropy(q: Sequence[RMatrix], v: Sequence[Fraction]) -> float:
    return sum(eta(born_weight(qa, v)) for qa in q)


def coarse_grain(q: Sequence[RMatrix], f: Sequence[int]) -> List[RMatrix]:
    """Merge channels: (f_* Q)_k = sum over {a : f(a) = k} of Q_a."""
    n = len(q[0])
    out: Dict[int, RMatrix] = {}
    for a, qa in enumerate(q):
        out[f[a]] = r_add(out.get(f[a], r_zero(n)), qa)
    return [out[k] for k in sorted(out)]


def demo_entropy() -> None:
    banner("6.  Observed Born measure and entropy monotonicity under coarse-graining")

    # A 4-dimensional PVM with four rank-1 orthogonal channels (diagonal, hence
    # symmetric, so the Born weights are genuine probabilities).
    n = 4
    q: List[RMatrix] = []
    for i in range(n):
        m = r_zero(n)
        m[i][i] = Fraction(1)
        q.append(m)

    ok, parts = is_real_pvm(q)
    print("the fine family is a PVM:", ok, parts)
    print("all channels symmetric  :", all(r_transpose(qa) == qa for qa in q))

    # The exactly normalized state v = (1/2, 1/2, 1/2, 1/2), giving the uniform
    # Born distribution (1/4, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4).
    v = [Fraction(1, 2)] * 4
    print("\nstate v =", [str(x) for x in v],
          " with |v|^2 =", sum((x * x for x in v), Fraction(0)))
    p = [born_weight(qa, v) for qa in q]
    print("Born weights:", [str(x) for x in p], " sum =", sum(p, Fraction(0)))

    h_fine = observed_entropy(q, v)
    print(f"\nfine entropy   H = {h_fine:.6f}   (= log 4 = {math.log(4):.6f})")

    # (a) merge two channels of positive weight  -> strict decrease
    f_merge = [0, 0, 1, 2]
    qc = coarse_grain(q, f_merge)
    h_c = observed_entropy(qc, v)
    print(f"\n(a) merging channels 1,2 (both weight 1/4 > 0):")
    print(f"    coarse entropy H' = {h_c:.6f}   strict decrease: {h_c < h_fine}")
    print(f"    predicted:  H' = {-0.5 * math.log(0.5) - 2 * 0.25 * math.log(0.25):.6f}")

    # (b) merge a positive-weight channel with a zero-weight channel -> equality
    v2 = [Fraction(1), Fraction(0), Fraction(0), Fraction(0)]
    p2 = [born_weight(qa, v2) for qa in q]
    print(f"\n(b) state v = {[str(x) for x in v2]}, Born weights {[str(x) for x in p2]}")
    h_fine2 = observed_entropy(q, v2)
    h_c2 = observed_entropy(coarse_grain(q, f_merge), v2)
    print(f"    fine H = {h_fine2:.6f},  coarse H' = {h_c2:.6f},  equality: {h_c2 == h_fine2}")
    print("    (equality boundary: no two channels of NONZERO weight were merged)")

    # (c) total merge into one channel -> entropy 0
    f_total = [0, 0, 0, 0]
    h_c3 = observed_entropy(coarse_grain(q, f_total), v)
    print(f"\n(c) merging everything into one channel: H' = {h_c3:.6f} "
          f"(<= {h_fine:.6f}: {h_c3 <= h_fine})")

    # Sharp criterion check across all merging schemes of a 4-element set.
    print("\nSharp equality criterion, checked over all 4^4 merging schemes:")
    bad = 0
    for code in range(4 ** 4):
        f = [(code >> (2 * i)) & 3 for i in range(4)]
        hc = observed_entropy(coarse_grain(q, f), v)
        pw = [born_weight(qa, v) for qa in q]
        no_merge_of_positives = all(
            not (f[a] == f[b] and a != b and pw[a] != 0 and pw[b] != 0)
            for a in range(4) for b in range(4))
        equal = abs(hc - h_fine) < 1e-12
        if equal != no_merge_of_positives:
            bad += 1
    print(f"   schemes violating the criterion: {bad}   (0 means the criterion is exact)")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 6: the functional calculus survives observation
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_functional_calculus() -> None:
    banner("7.  Polynomial functional calculus: st(p(A)) = p(st(A))")

    a = hyper_matrix([[Hyper.real(2) + EPS, Hyper.real(1)],
                      [Hyper.real(-1) * EPS, Hyper.real(3)]])
    print("A =", fmt_hyper_matrix(a), "   (finite entries)")

    # p(X) = X^3 - 2X + 5
    def p_hyper(m: HMatrix) -> HMatrix:
        m2 = h_mul(m, m)
        m3 = h_mul(m2, m)
        out = h_sub(m3, h_smul(Hyper.real(2), m))
        return h_add(out, h_smul(Hyper.real(5), h_identity(len(m))))

    def p_real(m: RMatrix) -> RMatrix:
        m2 = r_mul(m, m)
        m3 = r_mul(m2, m)
        out = [[m3[i][j] - 2 * m[i][j] for j in range(len(m))] for i in range(len(m))]
        return r_add(out, [[5 * x for x in row] for row in r_identity(len(m))])

    lhs = st_matrix(p_hyper(a))
    rhs = p_real(st_matrix(a))
    print("p(X) = X^3 - 2X + 5")
    print("st(p(A)) =", fmt_real_matrix(lhs))
    print("p(st A)  =", fmt_real_matrix(rhs))
    print("equal    :", lhs == rhs)

    # Approximate annihilators become exact: B^2 - B is infinitesimal.
    b = hyper_matrix([[ONE, EPS], [ZERO, EPS * EPS]])
    b2mb = h_sub(h_mul(b, b), b)
    print("\nB =", fmt_hyper_matrix(b))
    print("B^2 - B =", fmt_hyper_matrix(b2mb), " infinitesimal:",
          is_infinitesimal_matrix(b2mb))
    sb = st_matrix(b)
    print("st(B) =", fmt_real_matrix(sb), " and st(B)^2 - st(B) = 0 exactly:",
          r_mul(sb, sb) == sb)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def main() -> None:
    print(__doc__)
    demo_eps_channel()
    demo_sharpness_if_direction()
    demo_sharpness_only_if_direction()
    demo_three_channel_quantization()
    demo_spectral_collapse()
    demo_entropy()
    demo_functional_calculus()
    banner("All demonstrations completed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

demos.name: Randomized Exact-Arithmetic Stress Test of the Observation Correspondence
demos.description: A statistical audit of every theorem in the development, run on randomly generated data in exact rational and symbolic arithmetic. Each trial builds a random symmetric projection-valued measure on R^n by conjugating a random block-diagonal family of coordinate projections with a rational Householder reflection, then perturbs every single entry by a random infinitesimal of random order, so that the resulting hyperreal family satisfies none of the measurement identities exactly. The trial then verifies, without any floating-point arithmetic except in the entropy comparisons, that the perturbed family is an approximate projection-valued measure, that observation recovers the original measure on the nose, that idempotency -- which is never assumed -- holds up to infinitesimals, that the observed ranks and traces quantize and sum to the dimension, that the exact model supplied by rigidity is genuinely exact and sits at infinitesimal distance, that the observed Born weights are nonnegative and sum to one, and that observed entropy is monotone under random merging schemes with equality exactly on the predicted set. Sixty trials in dimensions two through five pass every check.

algorithms.name: Exact Symbolic Representation of the Observation Map
algorithms.description: The observation map is the entrywise standard part, which is only well behaved on matrices with no infinite entry; to compute with it one needs a representation of hyperreals in which 'infinite', 'appreciable' and 'infinitesimal' are decidable. We represent a hyperreal exactly as a finite Laurent series in a formal infinite element w with rational coefficients, x = sum_k c_k w^k. Then x is infinite exactly when some c_k with k > 0 is nonzero, infinitesimal exactly when all c_k with k >= 0 vanish, and otherwise finite with standard part c_0. This makes the three predicates exact decisions rather than numerical thresholds, which matters because the whole theory turns on distinguishing an infinitesimal from a small real number. Observing an n x n matrix costs O(n^2 K) coefficient inspections when each entry carries at most K terms; the canonical lift in the reverse direction costs the same and satisfies st(lift(M)) = M, making it a section of observation.
algorithms.pseudocode:
REPRESENT  x  as a finite map  k -> c_k  (rational), meaning  sum_k c_k w^k

function IS-INFINITE(x)
    return TRUE if c_k != 0 for some k > 0, else FALSE

function IS-INFINITESIMAL(x)
    return TRUE if c_k  = 0 for all k >= 0, else FALSE

function ST(x)
    if IS-INFINITE(x) then return 0          // convention; never used in theorems
    return c_0

function ST-MATRIX(A)                        // the observation map
    for i = 1..n, j = 1..n
        B[i][j] <- ST(A[i][j])
    return B

function LIFT(M)                             // canonical section of observation
    for i = 1..n, j = 1..n
        A[i][j] <- the series with single coefficient c_0 = M[i][j]
    return A

PRECONDITION for ST-MATRIX to be a ring homomorphism:
    NOT IS-INFINITE(A[i][j]) for every i, j

algorithms.name: The Certified Descent Test for Hyperreal Projection-Valued Measures
algorithms.description: This is the Descent Theorem turned into a decision procedure. Given a finite family of hyperreal matrices, it checks the three hypotheses -- finiteness of all entries, orthogonality of distinct channels up to infinitesimals, and completeness up to infinitesimals -- and returns, alongside the verdict, a certificate consisting of the observed channels, their ranks, and the quantization identity stating that the ranks sum to the dimension. Because the theorem is an equivalence under finiteness, the test needs no separate check that the observation is a measurement: the three hypotheses decide it. The test also reports when finiteness fails, since in that regime the equivalence is genuinely false in both directions and no conclusion may be drawn. The dominant cost is the O(m^2) symbolic matrix products for m channels, each O(n^3) coefficient convolutions of length O(K), giving O(m^2 n^3 K) exact rational operations; the rank computations add only O(m n^3). All arithmetic is exact, so the procedure never mistakes a genuinely small real number for an infinitesimal.
algorithms.pseudocode:
input:  P[1..m], hyperreal n x n matrices in exact Laurent representation
output: a descent certificate

1.  FINITE <- for all a, i, j:  NOT IS-INFINITE(P[a][i][j])

2.  ORTHOGONAL <- TRUE
    for a = 1..m, for b = 1..m with b != a
        C <- SYMBOLIC-MATRIX-PRODUCT(P[a], P[b])
        if some entry of C is not infinitesimal then ORTHOGONAL <- FALSE

3.  D <- (P[1] + ... + P[m]) - I
    COMPLETE <- every entry of D is infinitesimal

4.  Q[a] <- ST-MATRIX(P[a])  for a = 1..m       // the observation

5.  DESCENDS <- (Q is idempotent, pairwise orthogonal and sums to I)
    // by the Descent Theorem, if FINITE then
    //     DESCENDS  <==>  (ORTHOGONAL and COMPLETE)

6.  if DESCENDS then
        r[a] <- RANK(Q[a])                      // exact Gaussian elimination
        assert r[1] + ... + r[m] = n            // quantization certificate

7.  return (FINITE, ORTHOGONAL, COMPLETE, DESCENDS, Q, r)

algorithms.name: Rigid Exact-Model Reconstruction of an Approximate Measurement
algorithms.description: Rigidity says that every finite-entry approximate hyperreal projection-valued measure lies entrywise infinitesimally close to an exact one -- a family satisfying idempotency, orthogonality and completeness with no slack whatsoever. The remarkable computational content is that the exact model requires no search, no iteration and no linear solve: it is the canonical lift of the family's own observation. The reason is that observation is a ring homomorphism on finite-entry matrices, so the exact identities of the observed real family are inherited entrywise by the lift, while lifting inverts observing, placing the model in the same infinitesimal halo. The routine builds the model in O(m n^2 K) operations, re-verifies its three exact identities in O(m^2 n^3) operations as a safeguard, and returns the discrepancy matrices together with a proof-shaped certificate that every one of their entries is infinitesimal. If the input family is additionally approximately symmetric, the very same model is exactly symmetric, giving an exact orthogonal resolution of the identity.
algorithms.pseudocode:
input:  P[1..m], an approximate hyperreal PVM with finite entries
output: an exact hyperreal PVM R with P[a] - R[a] infinitesimal for all a

1.  for a = 1..m
        Q[a] <- ST-MATRIX(P[a])           // observe
        R[a] <- LIFT(Q[a])                // re-embed; no search is needed

2.  VERIFY (safeguard, not part of the construction):
        for a:            R[a] * R[a]  =  R[a]           exactly
        for a != b:       R[a] * R[b]  =  0              exactly
                          R[1] + ... + R[m]  =  I        exactly

3.  for a = 1..m
        DELTA[a] <- P[a] - R[a]
        assert every entry of DELTA[a] is infinitesimal

4.  if every P[a] is approximately symmetric then
        R[a] is exactly symmetric                        // orthogonal model

5.  return (R, DELTA)

UNIQUENESS: if R and R' are both lifts of real families and lie in the same
halo, then R = R'; so the model returned here is the only lifted exact model.

algorithms.name: Observed Spectral Collapse by Coarse-Graining of Eigenvalues
algorithms.description: Given a hyperreal spectral decomposition A = sum_a lambda_a P_a with finite eigenvalues and finite-entry channels, a real observer cannot see the individual channels whose eigenvalues differ only by an infinitesimal: their spectral lines coincide after observation, and only the sum of their projections is recoverable. This algorithm computes the observed operator together with its genuine real spectral decomposition, by observing each eigenvalue, grouping the indices into the fibres of the map 'observed eigenvalue', and summing the observed projections within each fibre. Because merging channels of a measurement again yields a measurement, the merged projections form a bona fide real projection-valued measure whose ranks sum to the dimension. The cost is one observation pass, O(m n^2 K), one grouping, O(m log m), and one accumulation, O(m n^2). The output makes the resolution limit explicit: the number of observed lines is the number of distinct standard parts among the eigenvalues, which may be strictly smaller than the number of hyperreal lines.
algorithms.pseudocode:
input:  lambda[1..m] finite hyperreal eigenvalues
        P[1..m]      finite-entry hyperreal channels
output: st(A) and its observed spectral lines

1.  assert NOT IS-INFINITE(lambda[a]) for all a

2.  for a = 1..m
        mu[a] <- ST(lambda[a])                  // observed eigenvalue
        Q[a]  <- ST-MATRIX(P[a])                // observed channel

3.  GROUPS <- empty map from real numbers to matrices
    for a = 1..m
        GROUPS[mu[a]] <- GROUPS[mu[a]] + Q[a]   // fibrewise sum: coarse-graining

4.  LINES <- sorted list of (mu, GROUPS[mu], RANK(GROUPS[mu]))

5.  OBSERVED <- sum over LINES of mu * GROUPS[mu]
    // equals ST-MATRIX(sum_a lambda[a] * P[a])

6.  return (OBSERVED, LINES)

COLLAPSE: |LINES| = number of distinct standard parts of the eigenvalues,
which is < m exactly when two eigenvalues differ by an infinitesimal.

visualizations.name: Halo Collapse and the Quantization of Observed Traces
visualizations.description: A two-panel figure explaining the two faces of observation. The left panel draws the hyperreal line above the real line: each real number carries a halo of hyperreals infinitely close to it, and the standard part crushes each halo to its centre, so that any two points of a halo become literally indistinguishable after observation; an infinite element is shown escaping off the right edge, with no shadow at all, which is exactly the situation in which the theory's hypotheses fail. The right panel makes dimension quantization visible: the hyperreal traces of the channels of an approximate measurement on a six-dimensional space scatter through the halos of the integers, while the observed traces are forced onto the natural numbers 3, 2, 1, 0, which sum exactly to the dimension six.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualization: the halo collapse and the quantization of observed traces.

Left panel: the hyperreal line seen through a magnifying glass.  Each real
number carries a halo of hyperreals infinitely close to it; the observation map
(the standard part) crushes every halo to its centre.  Points that differ by an
infinitesimal are indistinguishable after observation, while an infinite entry
falls off the picture entirely.

Right panel: dimension quantization.  The hyperreal traces of the channels of
an approximate projection-valued measure scatter through the halos of the
integers; observation snaps each of them to a natural number, and the numbers
sum to the dimension of the space.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List, Tuple

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def halo_scatter(centre: float, count: int, spread: float,
                 rng: np.random.Generator) -> np.ndarray:
    """Points scattered inside the (visually exaggerated) halo of `centre`."""
    return centre + rng.uniform(-spread, spread, size=count)


def main() -> None:
    rng = np.random.default_rng(20260907)
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13.5, 5.4))

    # ---------------- Left: halos and their collapse ----------------------
    centres: List[float] = [-1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0]
    spread = 0.14
    for c in centres:
        halo = halo_scatter(c, 22, spread, rng)
        ax1.scatter(halo, np.full_like(halo, 1.0), s=16, alpha=0.55,
                    color="#4c72b0", zorder=3)
        ax1.add_patch(plt.Circle((c, 1.0), spread, transform=ax1.transData,
                                 fill=True, alpha=0.10, color="#4c72b0", zorder=1))
        for h in halo[:8]:
            ax1.annotate("", xy=(c, 0.05), xytext=(h, 0.95),
                         arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", lw=0.5, alpha=0.30,
                                         color="#4c72b0"))
        ax1.scatter([c], [0.0], s=70, color="#c44e52", zorder=4)

    ax1.axhline(1.0, color="0.75", lw=1.0, zorder=0)
    ax1.axhline(0.0, color="0.35", lw=1.4, zorder=0)
    ax1.set_yticks([0.0, 1.0])
    ax1.set_yticklabels(["real line  $\\mathbb{R}$", "hyperreal line  $\\mathbb{R}^*$"])
    ax1.set_ylim(-0.45, 1.65)
    ax1.set_xlim(-1.7, 2.9)
    ax1.set_xticks(centres)
    ax1.set_title("Observation collapses every halo to a point\n"
                  "$\\mathrm{st}(x+\\varepsilon)=\\mathrm{st}(x)$ for all infinitesimal "
                  "$\\varepsilon$", fontsize=11)

    # the infinite element falls off the right edge
    ax1.annotate("$\\omega$  (infinite: no shadow)", xy=(2.82, 1.0), xytext=(1.75, 1.42),
                 fontsize=10, color="#8172b2",
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#8172b2", lw=1.3))
    ax1.scatter([2.82], [1.0], s=80, marker=">", color="#8172b2", zorder=5)

    # ---------------- Right: quantization of observed traces --------------
    # Four channels of an approximate PVM on R^6 with observed ranks 3, 2, 1, 0.
    true_ranks = [3, 2, 1, 0]
    labels = [f"channel {i + 1}" for i in range(len(true_ranks))]
    jitter = [0.11, -0.08, 0.13, 0.06]  # exaggerated pictures of infinitesimals
    hyper_traces = [r + j for r, j in zip(true_ranks, jitter)]

    xs = np.arange(len(true_ranks))
    ax2.bar(xs - 0.19, hyper_traces, width=0.36, color="#4c72b0", alpha=0.75,
            label="hyperreal trace  $\\mathrm{tr}\\,P_a$  (continuum-valued)")
    ax2.bar(xs + 0.19, true_ranks, width=0.36, color="#c44e52", alpha=0.85,
            label="observed trace  $\\mathrm{st}(\\mathrm{tr}\\,P_a)=\\mathrm{rank}\\,"
                  "\\mathrm{st}(P_a)\\in\\mathbb{N}$")
    for k in range(0, 5):
        ax2.axhline(k, color="0.85", lw=0.8, zorder=0)
    for x, (h, r) in enumerate(zip(hyper_traces, true_ranks)):
        ax2.annotate(f"{h:+.2f}".replace("+", ""), (x - 0.19, h + 0.08),
                     ha="center", fontsize=8, color="#37527a")
        ax2.annotate(str(r), (x + 0.19, r + 0.08), ha="center", fontsize=9,
                     color="#8c2f33", weight="bold")

    ax2.set_xticks(xs)
    ax2.set_xticklabels(labels)
    ax2.set_ylabel("trace")
    ax2.set_ylim(-0.35, 4.0)
    ax2.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8.5, framealpha=0.95)
    ax2.set_title("Dimension quantization on $\\mathbb{R}^6$:\n"
                  f"observed traces are integers and "
                  f"{' + '.join(map(str, true_ranks))} = {sum(true_ranks)} = "
                  "$\\dim\\mathbb{R}^6$", fontsize=11)

    fig.suptitle("The shadow of a non-Archimedean measurement", fontsize=13.5,
                 weight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.94))
    fig.savefig("halo_collapse_and_quantization.png", dpi=170)
    print("wrote halo_collapse_and_quantization.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

visualizations.name: The Entropy Ledger of Coarse-Graining and its Sharp Equality Boundary
visualizations.description: A two-panel figure quantifying the information destroyed when measurement channels are merged. The left panel takes a two-outcome observed Born distribution (t, 1-t) and plots the fine entropy against the entropy after merging the two outcomes into one, which is identically zero; the shaded region between them is the information destroyed, and the two curves touch exactly at t = 0 and t = 1, precisely the configurations in which no two channels of nonzero weight are being merged. The right panel enumerates all 256 merging schemes of a four-outcome measurement with observed weights (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8), plots the resulting entropies in sorted order, and colours each scheme by how many distinct positive-weight channels its largest block merges. No point rises above the fine entropy, and the 24 schemes attaining equality are exactly the 24 that keep the positive-weight channels apart -- the sharp criterion, verified by exhaustion.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualization: the entropy cost of merging measurement channels.

Left panel: the two-channel picture.  Merging the two channels of a measurement
whose observed Born distribution is $(t, 1-t)$ collapses the entropy to zero,
while the unmerged entropy is $-t\\log t-(1-t)\\log(1-t)$.  The two curves touch
exactly at $t\\in\\{0,1\\}$ — precisely the configurations in which no two
channels of *nonzero* weight are being merged.  This is the equality boundary
of the entropy monotonicity theorem, drawn.

Right panel: every merging scheme at once.  For a four-outcome measurement with
observed Born weights $(1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8)$ we enumerate all $4^4 = 256$ maps
of the index set into a four-element set, compute the entropy of the merged
distribution, and colour each scheme by how many distinct positive-weight
channels its largest block merges.  No point ever rises above the fine entropy,
and equality occurs exactly for the schemes that keep the positive-weight
channels separated.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def eta(t: float) -> float:
    return 0.0 if t <= 0.0 else -t * np.log(t)


def entropy(p: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return float(sum(eta(x) for x in p))


def merged(p: Sequence[float], f: Sequence[int]) -> List[float]:
    out: Dict[int, float] = {}
    for a, pa in enumerate(p):
        out[f[a]] = out.get(f[a], 0.0) + pa
    return [out[k] for k in sorted(out)]


def max_positives_in_a_block(p: Sequence[float], f: Sequence[int]) -> int:
    counts: Dict[int, int] = {}
    for a, pa in enumerate(p):
        if pa > 0:
            counts[f[a]] = counts.get(f[a], 0) + 1
    return max(counts.values(), default=0)


def main() -> None:
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13.5, 5.2))

    # -------- Left: the two-channel equality boundary ---------------------
    ts = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 801)
    h_fine = np.array([entropy([t, 1.0 - t]) for t in ts])
    h_coarse = np.zeros_like(ts)

    ax1.fill_between(ts, h_coarse, h_fine, color="#dd8452", alpha=0.22,
                     label="entropy destroyed by merging")
    ax1.plot(ts, h_fine, lw=2.4, color="#4c72b0",
             label="$H$ (two channels, weights $t,\\,1-t$)")
    ax1.plot(ts, h_coarse, lw=2.4, color="#c44e52",
             label="$H'$ (channels merged into one)")
    ax1.scatter([0.0, 1.0], [0.0, 0.0], s=70, zorder=5, color="#55a868",
                edgecolor="k", linewidth=0.6,
                label="equality: only one channel has nonzero weight")
    ax1.set_xlabel("$t$  (observed Born weight of the first channel)")
    ax1.set_ylabel("Shannon entropy (nats)")
    ax1.set_title("Merging two channels: $H' \\leq H$, strict whenever both\n"
                  "weights are positive", fontsize=11)
    ax1.legend(fontsize=8.6, loc="upper center")
    ax1.set_ylim(-0.05, 0.86)
    ax1.grid(alpha=0.25)

    # -------- Right: all 256 merging schemes ------------------------------
    p = [0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125]
    hf = entropy(p)
    xs: List[int] = []
    ys: List[float] = []
    cs: List[int] = []
    for f in itertools.product(range(4), repeat=4):
        xs.append(len(xs))
        ys.append(entropy(merged(p, f)))
        cs.append(max_positives_in_a_block(p, f))

    order = np.argsort(ys)
    ys_sorted = np.array(ys)[order]
    cs_sorted = np.array(cs)[order]

    palette = {1: "#55a868", 2: "#dd8452", 3: "#c44e52", 4: "#8172b2"}
    for k in sorted(palette):
        mask = cs_sorted == k
        if not mask.any():
            continue
        label = ("no two positive channels merged (equality)" if k == 1
                 else f"largest block merges {k} positive channels")
        ax2.scatter(np.arange(len(ys_sorted))[mask], ys_sorted[mask], s=17,
                    color=palette[k], alpha=0.85, label=label)

    ax2.axhline(hf, color="#4c72b0", lw=2.0, ls="--",
                label=f"fine entropy $H = {hf:.4f}$")
    ax2.set_xlabel("the $4^4 = 256$ merging schemes, sorted by resulting entropy")
    ax2.set_ylabel("entropy of the merged distribution (nats)")
    ax2.set_title("Observed Born weights $(1/2,\\,1/4,\\,1/8,\\,1/8)$:\n"
                  "no merging scheme ever increases the entropy", fontsize=11)
    ax2.legend(fontsize=8.4, loc="lower right")
    ax2.grid(alpha=0.25)

    fig.suptitle("Entropy monotonicity under coarse-graining, and its sharp "
                 "equality boundary", fontsize=13.5, weight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.93))
    fig.savefig("entropy_coarse_graining.png", dpi=170)
    print("wrote entropy_coarse_graining.png")
    n_eq = sum(1 for y, c in zip(ys, cs) if abs(y - hf) < 1e-12)
    n_pred = sum(1 for c in cs if c <= 1)
    print(f"schemes attaining equality: {n_eq}; schemes with no merged pair "
          f"of positive channels: {n_pred}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

interactive_demos.title: The Descent Laboratory: Build a Measurement out of Infinitesimals and Watch it Cast a Shadow
interactive_demos.description: An editable two-channel measurement whose matrix entries are hyperreal expressions: type ordinary numbers, infinitesimals (e, e2), infinite quantities (w, w2) and any combination such as '1 + 3e - 2w'. The laboratory parses each entry exactly into a Laurent series in the infinite element, forms the products and the total symbolically, and reports live on the three hypotheses of the Descent Theorem -- finiteness of the entries, orthogonality up to infinitesimals, and completeness up to infinitesimals -- displaying the actual cross-talk matrix and completeness defect so that the reader can see whether the error is infinitesimal or appreciable. It then shows the observation, checks whether it is a genuine projection-valued measure, prints the observed traces and ranks with the quantization certificate, and, when descent holds, exhibits the exact model guaranteed by rigidity together with the infinitesimal distance to it. Seven presets walk the reader through the whole theory: the lift of an ordinary measurement, an approximate measurement that is not exact, higher-order infinitesimal slack, both sharpness witnesses in which an infinite entry breaks the theorem in each direction, an appreciable error that the observer correctly detects, and an incomplete family. Two collapsible sections explain the underlying mechanism and the redundancy of idempotency.
interactive_demos.html:
The Descent Laboratory

Build a two-channel measurement whose matrix entries are hyperreal numbers — ordinary reals plus infinitesimals (written e, meaning a quantity smaller than every positive real) and infinite quantities (written w = 1/e). The laboratory checks the three hypotheses of the Descent Theorem and tells you exactly what a real-valued observer sees.

Presets

The hyperreal family

Entry syntax: a sum of terms such as 1, -2, 3/4, e (infinitesimal), 2e, e2 (= e²), w (infinite), -2/w, w2. Example: 1 + 3e - 2w.

The three hypotheses

What the observer sees

Why does any of this work? (click for the mechanism)

On matrices none of whose entries is infinite, the entrywise standard part is a ring homomorphism: st(A+B) = st(A)+st(B) and st(AB) = st(A) st(B). Every polynomial identity of matrix algebra therefore passes through observation untouched, which is why infinitesimal cross-talk and an infinitesimal completeness defect are invisible. Conversely, a finite-entry matrix is entrywise infinitesimal exactly when its observation is zero, which is why the criterion is an "if and only if".

Idempotency is never assumed. If the observed channels satisfy QaQb = 0 for a ≠ b and ∑Qb = I, then Qa = Qa ∑Qb = Qa² because every cross term dies. So the hypothesis list is minimal.

Finiteness of the entries is the one thing that cannot be dropped: the product w · (−2e) = −2 is an appreciable number manufactured from an infinite entry and an infinitesimal one, and entrywise observation destroys both factors. Try the two sharpness presets to see this break the theorem in each direction.

interactive_demos.title: Merging Channels: the Entropy Ledger
interactive_demos.description: A live accounting of the information destroyed when measurement channels are merged. Four sliders set the observed Born weights of a four-outcome measurement; a row of buttons assigns each channel to one of four blocks, defining an arbitrary merging scheme. The panel computes the fine and merged distributions with their per-outcome entropy contributions, draws them side by side on a canvas with an arrow marking the merge, and reports the fine entropy, the merged entropy, the exact number of nats destroyed, and a live check of the monotonicity inequality. Crucially, it also predicts the outcome before computing it: whenever two distinct channels of positive weight land in the same block the widget announces a strict loss and names the offending pair, and whenever no such pair exists it announces equality -- the sharp criterion, made tangible. Two collapsible sections give the one-line proof (monotonicity of the logarithm, no convexity machinery) and the measurement-theoretic background on where the Born weights come from and why symmetry of the projections is load-bearing.
interactive_demos.html:
Merging Channels: the Entropy Ledger

A non-Archimedean measurement, once observed, hands a real observer a probability distribution over its outcomes — the observed Born weights. Real detectors merge outcomes: two adjacent bins are lumped into one. Drag the weights, assign each channel to a block, and watch the exact price of merging. The theorem behind the ledger: merging never increases the entropy, the loss is strict as soon as two channels of positive weight land in the same block, and equality holds in precisely the opposite case.

Four channels, their weights, and the blocks they are merged into

channelobserved Born weightmerge into block

The ledger

Left: the fine distribution. Right: the merged distribution. Bar heights are probabilities; the number above each bar is its entropy contribution −p log p.
The one-line reason merging can only cost you (click to reveal)

Write S for the total weight of a block and p for the weight of one channel inside it, so 0 ≤ p ≤ S. Because the logarithm is increasing, log p ≤ log S, hence −p log S ≤ −p log p. Sum this over the channels of the block: the left side telescopes into −S log S, the entropy of the merged channel, and the right side is the total fine entropy of the block. Summing over blocks gives the theorem. The inequality is strict exactly when some channel in the block has 0 < p < S, i.e. when the block contains a second channel of positive weight. No convexity machinery is used anywhere.

Where do these weights come from? (click for the measurement-theoretic background)

An observed measurement on n-dimensional space is a family of matrices Qa that are idempotent (Qa² = Qa), mutually exclusive (QaQb = 0 for a ≠ b) and exhaustive (∑Qa = I). Given a unit vector v, the weight of channel a is pa = vTQav. Exhaustiveness makes the weights sum to one, and symmetry of the projections makes them nonnegative — since then vTQav = ‖Qav‖². Merging channels along a map f replaces Q by the block sums ∑f(a)=kQa, which is again a measurement, and pushes the weights forward to the block sums shown here.

Symmetry is not decoration: for the oblique idempotent with rows (1, −3) and (0, 0) and the state v = (1, 1)/√2 one gets weight −1, and no entropy statement survives.

interactive_layout:
# The Shadow of a Measurement ### A guided tour of what a real observer can see of an infinitely precise instrument --- ## 0. The question, in one sentence Suppose an instrument is *infinitely* precise — so precise that its errors are smaller than every positive real number, yet not exactly zero. You, the observer, can only read real numbers. **What survives the translation?** That question has a completely clean answer, and this page builds it up from nothing. By the end you will be able to look at a family of matrices with infinitesimal and infinite entries and say immediately what a finite observer records, whether the record is a legitimate measurement, how many dimensions each outcome consumes, and how much information is destroyed when outcomes are merged.
Prerequisite: what is a hyperreal number? (click if the word is new) The [hyperreal numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperreal_number) $\mathbb{R}^*$ form an ordered field that properly extends the real numbers. It contains: - every real number; - **infinitesimals**: nonzero elements $\varepsilon$ with $|\varepsilon| < 1/k$ for *every* positive integer $k$; - **infinite** elements such as $\omega = 1/\varepsilon$, larger in absolute value than every integer. A hyperreal is called *finite* if it is not infinite. The single fact that makes the whole subject work is this: **every finite hyperreal $x$ is infinitely close to exactly one real number**, called its *standard part* and written $\mathrm{st}(x)$. So $\mathrm{st}(3+\varepsilon) = 3$ and $\mathrm{st}(\varepsilon) = 0$. Infinite elements have no standard part; we set $\mathrm{st}$ to $0$ there by convention, and every theorem below carefully avoids relying on that convention. The construction is a standard piece of [nonstandard analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonstandard_analysis); nothing beyond the three bullet points above is needed here.
Prerequisite: what is a projection-valued measure? A measurement with finitely many outcomes on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is modelled by a family of square matrices $Q_1,\dots,Q_m$, one per outcome, satisfying three identities: $$Q_a Q_a = Q_a \quad (\text{each is a projection}),$$ $$Q_a Q_b = 0 \ \text{ for } a \ne b \quad (\text{outcomes are exclusive}),$$ $$Q_1 + \cdots + Q_m = I \quad (\text{some outcome always occurs}).$$ Such a family is called a [projection-valued measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projection-valued_measure). Geometrically it slices $\mathbb{R}^n$ into complementary subspaces: $Q_a$ projects onto a subspace $V_a$, distinct subspaces meet only at the origin, and together they fill the space. Notice that all three conditions are **polynomial identities** among matrices. That is the entire reason the theory below works.
--- ## 1. First contact: play with a measurement made of infinitesimals Before any theorem, get your hands dirty. Below you can type hyperreal expressions directly into a two-channel measurement — use `e` for an infinitesimal, `w` for an infinite quantity, and any combination such as `1 + 3e - 2w`. The laboratory computes everything symbolically and tells you what an observer sees. **Start with the preset "ε-channel".** Notice that the two channels genuinely overlap ($P_1P_2 \ne 0$) and their total genuinely differs from the identity — and yet the observation is a perfect measurement. Then try **"Sharpness I"**, where the family is *exactly* a measurement in the hyperreal world and yet its shadow is not. Something is going on with the entry $\omega$. {{interactive_demo:0}} Three things to try before reading on: 1. In the ε-channel preset, change the `e` to `0.001`. It is a small number, but it is *real*. Watch descent fail. **Infinitesimal is not the same as small.** 2. In the ε-channel preset, change `e` to `e2` or `3e + 2e2`. Descent still holds. The *order* of the infinitesimal never matters. 3. In "Sharpness I", change the entry `w` to `1`. Now everything is finite — and the family stops being an exact measurement, exactly as the theory demands. --- ## 2. Why anything survives at all Here is the whole mechanism, and it is smaller than you expect. On the finite hyperreals, the standard part is a **ring homomorphism**: $$\mathrm{st}(x+y) = \mathrm{st}(x)+\mathrm{st}(y), \qquad \mathrm{st}(xy) = \mathrm{st}(x)\,\mathrm{st}(y).$$ Now extend it to matrices entry by entry, writing $\mathrm{st}(A)$ for the real matrix with entries $\mathrm{st}(A_{ij})$. If $A$ and $B$ have no infinite entry, then each entry of $AB$ is a *finite sum of products of finite hyperreals*, so the standard part slides through both the sum and the products: $$\boxed{\ \mathrm{st}(AB) = \mathrm{st}(A)\,\mathrm{st}(B)\ }$$ **Every polynomial identity in matrix algebra therefore survives observation.** Idempotency, orthogonality and completeness are polynomial identities. That is the theorem.
The dual statement, which gives the converse direction A finite-entry matrix $A$ is entrywise infinitesimal **if and only if** $\mathrm{st}(A) = 0$; and two finite-entry matrices $A, B$ satisfy $A \approx B$ (entrywise infinitesimal difference) **if and only if** $\mathrm{st}(A) = \mathrm{st}(B)$. In other words, the fibres of observation are exactly the *infinitesimal halos*. This is what converts each half of the descent criterion into the other, making it an honest equivalence rather than a one-way implication.
Here is the picture to keep in your head. The left half shows observation collapsing each halo to its centre; the right half shows the consequence we will meet in section 5. {{visualization:0}} --- ## 3. The Descent Theorem Call a family $P_1,\dots,P_m$ of hyperreal matrices an **approximate projection-valued measure** if - **(F)** no entry of any $P_a$ is infinite; - **(O)** every entry of $P_aP_b$ is infinitesimal for $a \ne b$; - **(C)** every entry of $P_1+\cdots+P_m - I$ is infinitesimal. > **Descent Theorem.** Let $P_1,\dots,P_m$ be hyperreal $n\times n$ matrices satisfying (F). Then > $\mathrm{st}(P_1),\dots,\mathrm{st}(P_m)$ form a genuine projection-valued measure **if and only > if** (O) and (C) hold. Read both directions slowly, because both are surprising: - **"if"**: a leaky detector whose cross-talk is below every finite threshold is observed as a *perfect* detector. Nothing needs to be repaired or idealized. The shadow does the repair. - **"only if"**: if the shadow is a perfect measurement, the original must have been infinitesimally perfect. There is no way to be visibly wrong and invisibly right.
Where did idempotency go? It was never assumed — click to see why it is free. Look at the hypothesis list: (O) and (C) are exclusivity and completeness, but $P_a^2 \approx P_a$ is nowhere to be found. It is not an oversight; it is a *consequence*. At the real level the argument is two lines. If $Q_aQ_b = 0$ for $a\ne b$ and $\sum_b Q_b = I$, then $$Q_a \;=\; Q_a I \;=\; Q_a\Big(\sum_b Q_b\Big) \;=\; \sum_b Q_aQ_b \;=\; Q_aQ_a,$$ because every cross term dies. Pull this back through the descent theorem and you learn that any finite-entry family satisfying (O) and (C) automatically satisfies $P_aP_a \approx P_a$. So the hypothesis list of the Descent Theorem is **minimal**: nothing was assumed that could have been derived, and neither of (O), (C) follows from the other. (Take a single channel $P_1 = 2I$: (O) holds vacuously, (C) fails. Take two channels $P_1 = P_2 = \tfrac12 I$: (C) holds, but $P_1P_2 = \tfrac14 I$ is not infinitesimal.)
The theorem is a decision procedure, and here it is as one: {{algorithm:1}}
The exact arithmetic underneath the test (click for the representation) To decide "infinitesimal" versus "small real" you cannot use floating point. The trick is to represent a hyperreal as a finite Laurent series in a *formal* infinite element $\omega$ with rational coefficients, $x = \sum_k c_k\omega^k$. Then $x$ is infinite exactly when some $c_k$ with $k>0$ is nonzero, infinitesimal exactly when all $c_k$ with $k \ge 0$ vanish, and otherwise finite with $\mathrm{st}(x) = c_0$. Three exact decisions, no thresholds. {{algorithm:0}}
--- ## 4. Where it breaks: infinite entries, and only infinite entries The finiteness hypothesis (F) looked like technical hygiene. It is in fact the entire content. Both directions of the theorem collapse without it, and both counterexamples fit on one line. **Against "if".** Consider $$P = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & \omega \\ -2/\omega & -1\end{pmatrix}.$$ Its top-left entry squared is $4 + \omega\cdot(-2/\omega) = 4 - 2 = 2$, and the other three entries work out the same way, so $P^2 = P$ **exactly**. The pair $(P, I-P)$ is a flawless hyperreal measurement. But $\mathrm{st}(P) = \mathrm{diag}(2,-1)$, which squares to $\mathrm{diag}(4,1)$. The shadow of a perfect measurement is imperfect. **Against "only if".** In one dimension take the family $(1, \omega)$. Its shadow is $(1,0)$, a perfectly good measurement — yet the product of the two channels is $\omega$, about as far from infinitesimal as a number gets.
The mechanism, in one sentence $\omega \cdot (-2/\omega) = -2$ is an **appreciable** quantity manufactured from an infinite entry and an infinitesimal one. Entrywise observation sends both factors to zero and loses the contribution — which is precisely the failure of multiplicativity of $\mathrm{st}$ off the finite part. The failure mode is not vagueness; it is **dynamic range**.
Go back to the laboratory in section 1 and load both sharpness presets. Watch the verdict box change its tone: it stops claiming the theorem and starts warning you that you have left its domain. --- ## 5. Quantization out of nowhere Now the result that has no counterpart in ordinary linear algebra intuition. Attach to each channel its **observed weight**: the standard part of its trace. > **Dimension Quantization.** For any approximate hyperreal projection-valued measure, each observed > weight is a *natural number* — the rank of the observed projection — and the weights sum exactly > to $n$, the dimension of the space. The hyperreal traces are continuum-valued: they can be $1+\varepsilon$, $2-3\varepsilon^2$, $0+\varepsilon$, anything in the halo of an integer. Observation snaps them to a lattice. The right panel of the figure in section 2 shows exactly this.
Why a projection's trace is its rank (click for the proof) If $Q^2 = Q$ then the linear map it induces is the projection onto its range along its kernel, so $\mathbb{R}^n = \mathrm{range}(Q) \oplus \ker(Q)$. In a basis adapted to this splitting $Q$ is $\mathrm{diag}(1,\dots,1,0,\dots,0)$ with exactly $\dim\mathrm{range}(Q)$ ones. Trace is basis-independent, so $\mathrm{tr}\,Q = \mathrm{rank}\,Q$. Now sum over the channels: $\sum_a \mathrm{rank}\,Q_a = \sum_a\mathrm{tr}\,Q_a = \mathrm{tr}\big(\sum_a Q_a\big) = \mathrm{tr}(I) = n$.
There is a geometric restatement. The observed channels carve the space into subspaces $V_a = \mathrm{range}\,\mathrm{st}(P_a)$ that are pairwise independent and jointly spanning: $$\mathbb{R}^n = V_1 \oplus V_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus V_m, \qquad \dim V_1 + \cdots + \dim V_m = n.$$ **The observable content of a non-Archimedean measurement is exactly an integral direct sum decomposition of the real space.** Nothing more, nothing less. --- ## 6. Rigidity: the approximate world is a thin skin on the exact one Is the hyperreal theory genuinely richer than the real one? Yes — but only just. It is *strictly* richer: the family $$P_1 = \begin{pmatrix}1&\varepsilon\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad P_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$$ has $P_1P_2 \ne 0$ and $P_1+P_2 \ne I$, so it is not an exact measurement, yet it is observed as one. (This is the ε-channel preset from section 1.) And yet: > **Rigidity Theorem.** Every approximate hyperreal projection-valued measure with finite entries > lies entrywise infinitesimally close to an **exact** one — a family satisfying all three > identities on the nose. The exact model is found by no search whatsoever. **Observe, then re-embed.** Because observation is multiplicative, the lift of the observed real family inherits the exact identities; because lifting inverts observing, it sits in the same infinitesimal halo. {{algorithm:2}}
The complete structural picture (click to see all four statements at once) Putting the results together, the observation map is completely understood: 1. **Surjective.** Every real projection-valued measure is observed from a hyperreal one — namely from its own lift, which is even exact. 2. **Fibres are halos.** Two finite-entry families are observed identically exactly when they are entrywise infinitesimally close. 3. **Every fibre meets the exact class.** Rigidity. And if the family is approximately symmetric, the exact model can be taken symmetric, giving an exact *orthogonal* resolution of the identity. 4. **The model is unique among lifts.** Two real families whose lifts are infinitesimally close are equal. So the approximate theory is the exact theory wearing an infinitesimally thin coat: strictly bigger, but with nothing new at any observable scale.
--- ## 7. Merging outcomes: spectral collapse and the price in entropy Real detectors coarse-grain. Given a map $f$ from fine outcomes to coarse ones, the merged channels are $Q'_k = \sum_{f(a)=k} Q_a$. Merging preserves the measurement axioms, and it commutes with observation — you may merge before or after observing, with the same result. This has a striking spectral consequence. If a hyperreal operator decomposes as $\sum_a \lambda_a P_a$ with finite eigenvalues, its shadow is $\sum_a \mathrm{st}(\lambda_a)\, \mathrm{st}(P_a)$, so **eigenvalues differing only by an infinitesimal are fused into a single observed spectral line**, with their projections summed. This is not a noise-limited resolution bound; it is a theorem. Infinitesimal spectral splitting is unobservable in principle. {{algorithm:3}} Merging costs information, and the cost is exactly quantifiable. Given a real unit vector $v$, the **Born weight** of channel $a$ is $p_a = v^{\mathsf T} Q_a v$. These are nonnegative when the projections are symmetric, and they sum to $1$, so they form an honest probability distribution. > **Entropy Monotonicity.** Merging never increases the [Shannon > entropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entropy_(information_theory)) $H = \sum_a -p_a\log p_a$ of > the observed distribution. The drop is *strict* as soon as two distinct channels of positive > weight are merged, and equality holds **exactly** when no two distinct channels of nonzero weight > are merged. Set the weights, choose a merging scheme, and watch the ledger. The widget predicts strictness or equality *before* computing the numbers, using the criterion above: {{interactive_demo:1}}
The one-line proof — no convexity machinery required Write $S$ for the total weight of a block and $p$ for the weight of one channel inside it, so $0 \le p \le S$. Since $\log$ is increasing, $\log p \le \log S$, hence $-p\log S \le -p\log p$. Sum over the channels of the block: the left side telescopes to $-S\log S$, the entropy of the merged channel, and the right side is the block's fine entropy. Summing over blocks gives the theorem. Strictness appears exactly when some channel in the block has $0 < p < S$ — that is, when the block contains a *second* channel of positive weight.
The equality boundary is sharp, and you can see it by exhaustion: {{visualization:1}}
Why symmetry of the projections is load-bearing, not decoration Nonnegativity of the Born weights uses symmetry: for a symmetric idempotent, $v^{\mathsf T}Q_a v = v^{\mathsf T}Q_a^{\mathsf T}Q_a v = \|Q_a v\|^2 \ge 0$. Drop it and the statement dies. The oblique idempotent $Q = \begin{pmatrix}1&-3\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ with $v = (1,1)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2$ gives weight $-1$, and no entropy statement survives negative "probabilities". Happily, symmetry descends for free: if $P_a^{\mathsf T} \approx P_a$ then $\mathrm{st}(P_a)$ is *exactly* symmetric.
--- ## 8. Run the whole theory yourself Everything above is verifiable in exact arithmetic, and the following script does it end to end: descent, both sharpness witnesses, quantization on a four-dimensional example, rigidity with its certified infinitesimal discrepancy, spectral collapse, entropy monotonicity checked against all $256$ merging schemes of a four-outcome measurement, and the polynomial functional calculus. {{demo:0}} And because a hand-picked example can flatter a theorem, here is the same set of claims audited on randomly generated data — random symmetric measurements built from rational Householder reflections, every entry perturbed by a random infinitesimal of random order, sixty trials in dimensions two through five: {{demo:1}} --- ## 9. What you now know An infinitely precise instrument reporting into a finite world transmits exactly one thing: **an integral orthogonal decomposition of the real space, together with a probability distribution on its pieces.** - Infinitesimal violations of the measurement axioms — leaky channels, sub-threshold cross-talk, an efficiency missing $1$ by an unmeasurable amount, infinitesimal asymmetry — are perfectly invisible, and the shadow repairs them for free. - The repair happens *only if* the violations were infinitesimal to begin with. The shadow is a faithful witness, not a whitewash. - Infinitesimally separated eigenvalues are fused. Continuum-valued spectral weights are snapped to integers summing to the dimension. - What is emphatically **not** invisible is infinite magnitude. A single unbounded entry can smuggle an appreciable quantity through a product and break the correspondence in either direction. The moral is worth stating plainly. Nonstandard analysis is usually advertised as a way to make limits look like algebra. What happens here is closer to the reverse: an *algebraic* structure — three polynomial identities among matrices — is pushed through a map that is emphatically not algebraic, the collapsing of an entire halo to a single point, and one asks what makes it through. The answer is: **everything polynomial, provided nothing is infinite.** Boundedness of the instrument, not exactness of its calibration, is the real hypothesis.
Further reading and connections - [Hyperreal numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperreal_number) and [nonstandard analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonstandard_analysis) — the number system and its logic, including the [transfer principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transfer_principle), which moves internal first-order statements between $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{R}^*$. Note that the standard part is *external*: it collapses a halo to a point, so every theorem above that mentions it lives outside the transfer-accessible fragment. - [Projection-valued measures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projection-valued_measure) and the [spectral theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem) — the classical home of resolutions of the identity. - [POVMs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/POVM) — the standard alternative response to imperfect measurements, which *weakens the algebra*. The approach here keeps the algebra intact and enlarges the field instead; rigidity shows the two are genuinely different moves, since an approximate hyperreal measurement is always infinitesimally close to an exact one. - [Shannon entropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entropy_(information_theory)) and [data processing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_processing_inequality) — the information- theoretic context for the coarse-graining results of section 7.
